subject: Computing adjoint for auto-diff variables in C++

messages.author: b998e9d6a5be0399
messages.subject: Computing adjoint for auto-diff variables in C++
parts:
Hello, and thank you ahead of time for your help. 

I am writing a C++ function, which I hope to contribute to stan/math. 

The function returns a random variable Y, and takes a combination of data and parameters as its input. If I understand correctly, Y and the parameters are auto-diff variables, with type stan::math::var.  

My function computes the value of Y, but it does not compute its adjoint. 

Will stan/math automatically compute the adjoint of Y if I stick to operators defined for autodiff variables? 
Do you recommend I template my function so that it deals both with variables of type double and stan::math::var? 

I am making these assumptions based on this conversation: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/contributing$20function$20C$2B$2B/stan-users/YxiFyUirPU4/ku23AQzJzjMJ

Clarification and suggestions are more than welcomed!

best,
charles

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Computing adjoint for auto-diff variables in C++
parts:
Hi Charles,

Welcome to the list.

On Thu, Nov 12, 2015 at 3:24 PM, charlesm93 <charles.ma...@gmail.com> wrote:
Hello, and thank you ahead of time for your help. 

I am writing a C++ function, which I hope to contribute to stan/math.

Great.

I've read through your email and I don't think you'll want to take that approach, but I could be mistaken. There needs to be some clarification: I'm still not sure what you're trying to do.

The function returns a random variable Y, and takes a combination of data and parameters as its input. If I understand correctly, Y and the parameters are auto-diff variables, with type stan::math::var.

I'll need some clarification with what you're calling a "random variable."


Is the function a random number generator where on multiple calls it's returning different values?
  or
Is the function returning a class of some sort that knows about its distribution and sufficient stats?
  or
Is the function a deterministic function of its inputs?

We don't have a "random variable" type in the Stan Math Library and my guess is that you're actually describing the third option.
My function computes the value of Y, but it does not compute its adjoint.

This is where I'm beginning to think it's the third option: a deterministic function of the inputs.

If you're only getting as far as computing the function value, my guess is that the function could be written in the Stan language and it'll be as fast as writing the function in C++ directly. Could you tell us what the function does?
Will stan/math automatically compute the adjoint of Y if I stick to operators defined for autodiff variables?
Yes.
Do you recommend I template my function so that it deals both with variables of type double and stan::math::var?

In order for the function to be useful in the Stan math library, it will need to template all arguments to the function this way.

It's the beauty of how the Stan language generates fully templated functions that allow any combination of autodiff variables (stan::math::var) and scalar constants (double; we don't get the gradients with respect to these arguments).
I am making these assumptions based on this conversation: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/contributing$20function$20C$2B$2B/stan-users/YxiFyUirPU4/ku23AQzJzjMJ
Sorry -- that's a really long thread and it feels out-of-date. Feel free to ask more questions!
Clarification and suggestions are more than welcomed!

I think what would help immensely is if you provided either a Stan function, some pseudocode, or even the C++ implementation that you have now.




Daniel

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Computing adjoint for auto-diff variables in C++
parts:
> On Nov 12, 2015, at 3:24 PM, charlesm93 <charles.ma...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hello, and thank you ahead of time for your help.
Thanks for moving the discussion over the mailing list.

> I am writing a C++ function, which I hope to contribute to stan/math.
>
> The function returns a random variable Y, and takes a combination of data and parameters as its input. If I understand correctly, Y and the parameters are auto-diff variables, with type stan::math::var.
>
> My function computes the value of Y, but it does not compute its adjoint.
>
> Will stan/math automatically compute the adjoint of Y if I stick to operators defined for autodiff variables?

Yes. But you don't get any added efficiency over defining
the function directly in Stan. What happens is the function
definition itself gets autodiffed at run time, which can take
up lots of memory and/or time compared to having analytic gradients.

For efficiency in reverse mode (what we use for gradients
in all of our algorithms) you can define your own vari instance
and use that instead. You can see how to do that in the autodiff
paper or in the code that gets compiled for user-defined functions
through the language.

Just make sure to promote the intermediate values you need.
> Do you recommend I template my function so that it deals both with variables of type double and stan::math::var?

Yes, see the section of the arXiv paper about promotion using
Boost. All the intermediate values have to be promoted to
the highest type, where math::var > double.

> I am making these assumptions based on this conversation: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/contributing$20function$20C$2B$2B/stan-users/YxiFyUirPU4/ku23AQzJzjMJ
>
> Clarification and suggestions are more than welcomed!

There's also a wiki page on how to add new user-defined functions
so that they are visible through the language. The key point is
adding to the symbol table. In that case, they absolutely need to
be definable so that any continuous variables can be instantiated
as either double or var or fvar (the reverse-mode autodiff).

- Bob

Hi Daniel, hi Bob,

thank you for your guidance, I trust it will be very helpful.

If you're only getting as far as computing the function value, my guess is that the function could be written in the Stan language and it'll be as fast as writing the function in C++ directly. Could you tell us what the function does?

I am writing a Pharmacometrics Model library, that contains "PRED" functions. These functions predict drug amounts in different compartments of the body during various events (dosing, observation, etc.) They are complex but widely used in the industry, hence the benefit of including them in stan/math. 

The library I am working on follows closely NONMEN and a similar library developed for BUGS (https://code.google.com/p/bugsmodellibrary/).
I'll need some clarification with what you're calling a "random variable."
As you guessed, the function is deterministic.
I think what would help immensely is if you provided either a Stan function, some pseudocode, or even the C++ implementation that you have now.

I will pinpoint some relevant code. The code as whole is a little bit long - it comprises a few files, which define classes, functors and many procedures. But first, I want to work on the advice you gave me. The code runs fine in C++ but, for reasons I am starting to understand, it is not Stan compatible yet. 

As Bob explained, I need to define the function so that it can be instantiated as double, var and fvar.  

I'll keep using this thread as more issues come up. 

- Charles

Hi Bob,

We're certainly aware of the work going on at both US and EU Novartis sites and have been in contact with Wenping and Sebastian. Our main reason for working on the development of such code is because the Novartis code is not publicly available and we do not know if and when it will be. In addition it's a useful exercise for us to learn Stan architecture.

Why program in C++ versus Stan? While Stan is a pretty rich programming language, C++ is more so. In particular it permits object-oriented approaches and a richer collection of data types that make it easier to deal with some of the complications of event schedules encountered in pharmacometric analyses. (Sorry for preaching to the converted.)

Thanks for your guidance and toleration of our struggles to grok Stan code.

Cheers,
Bill

In particular it permits object-oriented approaches and a richer collection of data types that make it easier to deal with some of the complications of event schedules encountered in pharmacometric analyses. That's reasonable, but it's really hard to make sense of the request when we don't know what computation is actually taking place.

Unfortunately, we haven't documented all of the internals of Stan, but there are some key requirements like the ability to instantiate the templated function under all combinations of double and stan::math::var that need to be met.

The effort of implementing functions in C++ level starts to pay off once you have analytic or at least computable gradients for each of the arguments of the function. Until then, I don't usually think it's worth the effort. With that said, if some functions are being used multiple times, the right place to focus would be to add a way to include functions using some sort of directive. We've looked into that, but it's just on our backburner.


With this particular function, it would really help to have some pseudo-code or a Stan function so we can try to understand the intention and provide better advice.
Thanks for your guidance and toleration of our struggles to grok Stan code.

If you run into anything questionable, please reach out and I'll help however I can.


Daniel

Cheers,
Bill

Dear all,
